column3: The Hebrew describes a stumbling person in the singular; BSB uses the plural.
The Hebrew leaves what comes upon him unnamed; BSB names trouble.
The Hebrew pictures anger through His nose or nostrils.
The Hebrew lists roar and voice without saying the lion may roar or growl.
The Hebrew uses a passive image of a word being stolen to him and has ear in the singular; BSB has ears.
The Hebrew says the multitude of his bones; BSB says all his bones.
The Hebrew names silence and a voice separately; BSB combines them as a whispering voice.
The Hebrew begins with behold, rather than BSB’s conditional if.
The Hebrew has an unnamed plural subject crushing them before a moth; BSB uses a passive and says like a moth.
The Hebrew has their tent cord in the singular; BSB uses cords.
